problem: Prior VLM navigation benchmarks (especially outdoor ones such as Touchdown, map2seq, StreetNav) rely on explicit step-by-step instructions and mostly single-city settings. They do not test whether VLMs can turn abstract, implicit human needs (e.g., 'I am thirsty') into grounded exploration in real open-world cities.
motivation: Real users express abstract goals that map to functional, spatial and semantic needs, which are not annotated on maps and require last-mile visual grounding. Humans solve this with cognitive maps, iterative observe-reason cycles, and recall of past experience, and current VLMs seem to lack these, so the paper builds a benchmark to expose the gap and probes human-inspired fixes.
key_idea: Introduce CitySeeker, a multi-city street-view benchmark for implicit-need-driven urban navigation with 6,440 trajectories, and analyze VLM bottlenecks through human-inspired Backtracking, Cognitive-map enrichment, and Retrieval memory (BCR) strategies.
insight: VLMs fail mainly through error accumulation over long horizons, weak spatial cognition and poor commonsense affordance inference, not just perception. The largest gains come from memory retrieval (R1 lifts Qwen2.5-VL-32B TCP from 19.9 to 26.9), and external progress signals (B2/B3) beat self-confidence backtracking, which even hurts small models (MiniCPM-V-2.6). Giving a global 2D map hurts task completion (Qwen2.5-VL-32B TCP 21.1 to 7.6) while improving nDTW, because models become map followers and fail to align map geometry with first-person views.
method: Benchmark construction: street-view panoramas from Google/Baidu placed as a graph with nodes every 20 m in Neo4j, POIs linked to nodes within 50 m, and need-to-POI mappings validated by a 120-person survey (83.39% consensus).
Route generation: A* shortest paths between start and target nodes with 5-25 steps, manually verified so the target POI is visible at the endpoint and no alternative POI lies along the path.

Navigation framework: ReAct-style Observe/Think/Act/Reflect loop over perspective views at each node, outputting a view index, confidence and a stop decision, with a 35-step limit and no memory between steps in the base setting.

Backtracking (B1/B2/B3): B1 reverts to the last trusted node when mean confidence over k=3 steps falls below 0.75; B2 triggers on topological distance to goal increasing for k=3 steps; B3 is B1 plus a hint giving the optimal action after the revert.

Spatial cognition enrichment (C1/C2): GPT-4.1 summarizes correct and erroneous trajectories from GPT-4o and Gemini-2.5-pro into a topology graph (C1) or a relative direction/distance description (C2) injected into the prompt.

Memory retrieval (R1/R2/R3): multi-round Neo4j memory, retrieved in the final round as a 1-hop topological subgraph (R1) or a 50 m spatial radius subgraph (R2); R3 appends the last 3 steps of intra-episode history to the context.
Evaluation protocol: TCE, TCP (within 50 m), TCC, SPL, SPD, nDTW and AS, over 27 zero-shot VLMs plus human, random and forward-only baselines.

setting.backbone: 27 off-the-shelf VLMs used zero-shot and frozen (GPT-4o, o4-mini, Gemini-2.5-pro, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, Llama-4, etc.); BCR studies use GPT-4o-mini, InternVL3-8B, MiniCPM-V-2.6, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-32B
setting.observation: street-view panorama at the current node split into perspective views per navigable heading, plus text instruction
setting.action_space: discrete choice of a perspective view / next graph node (20 m spacing), plus stop; up to 35 steps
setting.simulator: Custom graph-based street-view environment (Google/Baidu Street View panoramas in Neo4j); no physics simulator
setting.privileged: none for the base setting; B2 uses the ground-truth topological distance to goal and B3 uses shortest-path direction hints; C1/C2 memory is built from GT paths plus other models' trajectories; R1/R2 use memory from earlier rounds on the same query.

numbers.extra: map-free, no memory, 35-step limit; TCP uses 50 m threshold

numbers_note: Metrics use the paper's own names (TCE/TCP/TCC). Table 1's SPL column and Appendix Tables have per-category and per-threshold numbers not all copied here. BCR results use a 650-sample subset; the Table 2 baseline row for Qwen2.5-VL-32B is 19.9 TCP versus 21.1 on the full set.
results: All 27 VLMs perform poorly: the best, Qwen2.5-VL-32B, gets 21.1 TCP and 2.6 TCE, against 30.1 TCP for humans, and several models fall below the random baseline of 13.9 TCP. Performance drops with route length, Latent POI is the hardest category and Brand-Specific the easiest. BCR strategies help, with R1 giving Qwen2.5-VL-32B 26.9 TCP on the mini subset and combined B2/B3/C1/R3 reaching 27.38.
limitations: Base evaluation intentionally has no memory and is zero-shot; the BCR strategies were evaluated only on a 650-sample subset with a few models, and B2/B3/C1 use ground-truth or oracle-derived signals.
Benchmark is a discrete street-view graph without real dynamics, and images can't be redistributed (must be re-fetched via APIs); VLM latency and long-context cost limit real-time use.
The combined-BCR study is only preliminary, and no training or fine-tuning is explored; personalization is not addressed.
